text: Draw a chord across this circle at random. What's the chance it comes out longer than a side of this triangle? Pick a number. Joseph Bertrand published this puzzle in 1889 as a warning about two words, at random. Leave them vague, and one college can report an average class of 40 or 147. Start with the obvious simulation. Pick two points on the rim at random and join them. If the chord beats the triangle side, it turns gold. Run 10,000 chords and the gold share settles near point 33. Geometry agrees. Put a corner of the triangle on the first point. The chord is long only when the second point lands on this far arc, a third of the rim. Case closed until you code it a second way. Pick a random radius, a random point along it, and draw the chord through that point at right angles. This one settles near 0.5. A third program picks a random point anywhere inside, and makes it the chord's midpoint. That settles near 0.25. Bertrand printed all three, and wrote that none is wrong, and none is right. Each tally is good to about one percentage point. They disagree by 25 percentage points, and none of the code has a bug. One point sets a chord's length, its midpoint. Slide it outward and the cord shrinks. It matches the triangle's side when the midpoint is half a radius out, on the circle that fits inside the triangle. So a cord is long exactly when its midpoint lands in this gold circle. And each program is just a way of scattering midpoints Shrink every cord to its midpoint The midpoint program spreads them evenly so this circle with a quarter of the area catches a quarter of them The radius program spreads them evenly along the radius Where will they crowd? Toward the center. Every ring gets an equal share and inner rings are small. Half the radius, so one half. And the endpoints program piles them against the rim, so only a third land inside, the third we found. three programs three things spread evenly rim radius area at random never said which Edwin Janes argued that a physical process picks one straws tossed from a standing height can't be aimed so the answer can't depend on where the circle sits or how big it is one rain lands on both circles at once and each judges with its own gold circle so a fair recipe must score the same on both. Midpoint gives a quarter, then .41. Endpoints give a third, then .47. Only the radius program gives a half on both. Janes and Charles Tyler tossed real broom straws at a 5-inch circle, and the 128 that crossed it matched the radius program's flat spread. hide the same two words. Take classes of 10, 10, and 100. Pick a class at random, and the average size is 40. Pick a student at random, spread evenly over students instead of classes, and it's 85. At Stony Brook in 1974, those two picks gave 40, and 100 47. So whatever number you picked, some way of drawing chords makes it right. Name the way, and only one is. 40 and 147 are both right, once you say who's picked.
